At approximately 10:54 PM on March 1, 2025, in the county of Jefferson, I was dispatched to 4029 East Callaway Dr. in Rigby Idaho. The reporting party Millard Richard Farber (identified by his Alaska driver’s license). Stated that his wife, Kara J Farber (Identified by her Alaska driver’s license) was having a mental episode and was being very violent and was tearing up his truck and screaming and yelling. Millard stated that while he was on the phone, Kara jumped out of the truck and then took off running southeast of the residence in a blue down jacket that went down to her knees and black pants.

Upon arrival, I spoke briefly with Millard and he informed me of the situation and that pointed in an approximate direction of where Kara had run. I retrieved K9 Bizi from my patrol vehicle put him on a 30-foot-long line gave him the command to track and search for someone. We started going northeast of the property behind Millard‘s property. We continued to move northeast for approximately 25 yards and then we moved directly north all the while Bizi was moving in a serpentine pattern with his nose to the ground tracking when we hit the asphalt roadway Bizi had trouble picking back up the track. We moved across the roadway directly east then north, and then he picked a truck up and we went straight west from there for about 333 yards. Then we moved directly north for approximately 160 yards before moving North West until we hit the fairway of the golf course northeast of where we had started from the property at 4029 Callaway Dr.

Once Bizi and I were on the fairway of the golf course, we started moving east along the fairway until it slanted down going southeast. We moved southeast along the fairway of the golf course looking through the canal for approximately 265 yards. At which point Bizi yanked me down into the ditch and started pulling super hard at the end of the 30-foot line. Bizi pulled me approximately 25 yards and that’s when I saw Kara in the fetal position underneath a small footbridge north of 450 N. The small footbridge had a walking path from 450 North that took you onto the golf course. Bizi had tracked Kara from her home approximately three-quarters of a mile away.

Bizi was pulling super hard towards Kara. I started gathering the lineup and pulling him toward me while telling Kara to not move. While trying to get Bizi back to me, I asked for a secondary unit so I could control Bizi and get him away from Kara. Once I had Bizi back Heeled to my side I laid him down and started to communicate with Kara.

I told Kara that we had been out looking for her and I was concerned for her safety and well-being because of how cold it was that night her not having the proper clothing and her lying in the ditch. I asked Kara what was going on and she said that she was having marital problems and just did not want to be at the house. I asked if she was trying to hurt herself and she did not answer. I asked her to stand up come up to the bridge and go to 450 N. where we could await the arrival of my partners.

Deputy Hall arrived on scene and took Kara to his vehicle where she was detained for the time being. Deputy Black and Sgt Gonzales all arrived shortly after. And I informed them of what I knew at the time. Sgt. Gonzales asked Deputy Black to transport Kara back to her home where she could be placed in my patrol vehicle so I could take her to the hospital for a mental evaluation.

Once I got back to the home, I put Bizi back in my patrol vehicle and secured my tracking gear. I spoke with Kara, I informed her that her actions this evening were concerning, and because of the temperature and the weather outside being below freezing she had put herself in danger and wasn’t thinking in the right state of mind. I told Kara that she had two options she could willingly go to the hospital for a mental evaluation or the sheriff’s office would put her on a mental hold so that she could get a mental evaluation. I told Kara either way she was going to the hospital. Kara stated that she would willingly go to the hospital and speak with somebody and have a mental evaluation. I transported Kara to Eastern Idaho Regional Medical Center without incident and ensured that she was placed in a room to speak with a doctor. At approximately 2:00 A.M. Kara was transported by EIRMC security to the Behavioral Health Center (BHC). Nothing further at this time.

At approximately 1:21 AM on May 4, 2025, in the county of Jefferson, I was dispatched to a rolling disturbance on Highway 20 going southbound. The reporting party Catherine Jennings (identified by her Texas driver’s license) stated that John Jennings (identified by his Idaho driver's license) had beaten up his brother inside the vehicle and he was bleeding everywhere. His brother Andrew Martin Jennings (identified by his Texas driver's license). He was bleeding from his face, and Catherine stated that he was covered in blood. Dispatch had Catherine pull to the side of the road at mile marker 318 just past the southbound off-ramp. 

While I was en route, dispatch informed me that John was still causing problems inside the car and trying to cause fights. I asked the Rigby City Police Dept. due to the report given. When we were about a mile away from where they had pulled over, dispatch informed us that John had fled on foot northwest of where they were parked on Highway 20. They informed us that John was wearing a white tank top and khaki shorts. He had a red beard and red hair. Officer Hawkins arrived first on the scene and got out with Catherine and Andrew to check their medical status. Officer Hawkins immediately stated that he needed medical to come to his location.

Officer Bench and I started searching the area and I asked for Idaho State Police to assist us in locating the John. I started searching the commercial building complex Northwest of Highway 20 where Catherine had pulled off. Catherine stated that is the area that John started running towards. I searched through that area in my vehicle not able to locate John. When Deputy Condon arrived on the scene. I went back up towards Officer Hawkins where Catherine‘s vehicle was off the side of the road on Highway 20. Officer Hawkins informed me that Andrew was severely beaten was bleeding and had a cut below his eye and on his nose.

I deployed K9 Bizi on a 30-foot-long leash and gave him the command to track and search for a suspect, which was John in the open field directly west of the vehicle. Bizi started pulling me north up the fence line and then started pulling to the west where he started moving in his zigzag pattern and stuck his nose in the air. Bizi started pulling me north in the field with his nose in the air, moving in that zigzag pattern. As we moved further north, I saw something in the field. I pulled back on Bizi's leash and shined my light on the object that I saw. I quickly identified that it was a person and on further observation. I noticed that it was a person matching the description given to us. I called out the Sheriff’s office and told John to show me his hands and if he failed to do so he was going to get bit by the K9. John was lying on his stomach in the weeds next to a berm. He rolled over and put his hands up in the air still in his sitting position. I told him to stay still and keep his hands in the air. I noticed that my body cam was not activated, and I quickly activated it. John stated to me that he was done. He wasn’t going to run or cause problems. I kept Bizi at a safe distance and said when my partners get up here you’re not going to cause any problems and he said that he would not. Deputy Condon, Officer Bench and, Officer Hawkins approached. They gave John the command to roll over on his stomach put his hands behind his back and John complied. He was then handcuffed lifted to his feet and escorted to Officer Benches’ vehicle. I noticed that John had a cut above his eye and was shirtless. While Officer Bench and Deputy Condon were escorting John to their squad car I informed them to take him to the road and have medical come and check him out.

I returned, K9 Bizi to my squad car and then went up to speak with Catherine and Andrew. When I spoke with the pair, I noticed that Andrew’s left eye was severely swollen and bruising. He was covered in blood and had a cut below his left eye that was swollen. I asked the pair a few questions about what had happened and all they stated was that they got into a fight and they were brothers. At approximately 2:40 P.M. on 7/23/2025 in the county of Jefferson, SSgt Gonzales had me meet him at 4223 E 528 N, The LDS church parking lot, to stage to serve a felony warrant on Patrick Kent Burns (Identified by his Idaho driver's license). The informant told us that Patrick was staying in the northwest bedroom and was armed with a knife and possibly a firearm. 

While staging at the church, we created a team and assigned each unit a position to create a perimeter around the home. At 3:20 P.M., SSgt Melanese informed all units to move in on the home. SSgt Gonzales, Deputy Scott, and I all moved in on the residence and pulled into the driveway. I quickly pulled K9 Bizi from my vehicle and laid him down next to me while the other units got to their positions. Once all units were in position, I used my public address system (PA) to make announcements to Patrick that the Jefferson County Sheriff’s office had the home surrounded and that he needed to come out slowly with his hands up. I put out on the PA that there was a Sheriff K9 on the scene, and if he didn’t come out, that we would be sending the K9 into the home, and he would be bitten. I gave several announcements over the PA with no response or movement that I could see. Detective Vernon, positioned on the back side of the house, stated he could see movement in the northwest bedroom window, but it had ceased quickly. When there was no response, SSgt Gonzales took up my position while I took K9 Bizi to the south side of the home to meet up with SSgt Melanese and Detective Hammer. 

Once I met up with them, it was decided that K9 Bizi and I would move to a south-facing sliding glass door and give commands at the door. Detective Hammer, K9 Bizi, and I approached the home slowly and tactfully. I laid K9 Bizi outside the doorway, and I stood to the left of the doorway. I gave loud commands again, announcing Jefferson County Sheriff’s office. I continued with we have a warrant for your arrest, and there is a K9 that will be released into the home. Patrick would be bitten if he didn’t come out slowly with his hands up.  I gave three commands and awaited orders for my next step. I was instructed to release K9 Bizi into the home. I gave another command and released K9 Bizi into the home. 

K9 Bizi moved around the inside of the home. I could hear him searching the inside of the home, and heard him start scratching on something, but then returned to me. I gave K9 Bizi the command to search the home once again, and he reentered searching again. I again heard K9 Bizi scratch at something, then return to me. When K9 Bizi returned to me, I had him lie down outside the doorway while the officer in charge decided our next steps. Captain Williams arrived on the scene and informed the team to make entry with K9 Bizi and clear the home.  SSgt Gonzales, Detective Hammer, K9 Bizi, and I all entered the home slowly and cleared it methodically. K9 Bizi was in front of the team searching and pulled towards the hallway where Patrick was said to be. The team got to the hallway where I laid K9 Bizi down and gave further commands that he needed to come out, or he was going to get bitten. I gave several commands with no response. I released K9 Bizi down the hall where he sniffed around, then sniffed the door that Patrick was said to be behind and barked, indicating that someone was in the room. 

It was decided that the team was going to go down the hall and make entry into the room on the northwest side of the home, the room that Patrick was said to be in. We moved down the hallway, and as I got into position to kick the door open, I heard what sounded like the racking of an automatic rifle. This sound is distinct, and when I heard this, I pushed the team back down the hall and informed all other units what I had heard. We then held our positions in the hallway until Bonneville SWAT team could arrive and assist us in taking Patrick into custody safely. 

While holding the position inside the home, every five minutes, I gave announcements to Patrick to come out slowly, informing him that he had a warrant for his arrest. I never did hear a response from the room. Bonneville SWAT arrived and relieved SSgt Gonzales, Detective Hammer, K9 Bizi, and I. Once we were relieved, I took up a position to watch perimeter on the south side of the home while Bonneville SWAT tried negotiating with Patrick. Bonneville SWAT negotiated with Patrick for several hours before releasing chlorobenzylidene malononitrile (CS) gas into the home. Once CS was released into the room where Patrick was, he got out from under some blankets in a closet area where he had been hiding and surrendered to the SWAT deputies at 8:08 P.M. without further incident. 

Patrick was taken into custody and transported to Eastern Idaho Regional Medical Center (EIRMC) for a jail clearance. Deputy Black transported Patrick to the hospital, where he was cleared to be transported to the Jefferson County jail. Patrick was transported without incident. Nothing further at this time.

At approximately 12:19 AM on September 9, 2025, in the county of Jefferson. I was parked just south of the Menan-Lorenzo Highway, off the Yellowstone Highway, watching the stop sign as it went down towards the river and the train bridge. 

Earlier in the evening, we were dispatched to 703 Yellowstone Highway, the location of the train bridge, for a welfare check on an individual. When Deputy Hall arrived, an individual jumped from the train bridge and floated downriver. Deputy Hall went to check the welfare of this individual when he saw him on a small island in the middle of the river. The individual saw Deputy Hall and tried to hide. All Jefferson units and Central Fire units arrived on the scene to search for the individual and check his welfare. Deputy Black located a backpack on the train bridge where the individual had jumped from, with documents inside for David Randall Hicks, identified by his name and date of birth. Dispatch informed us that the individual had a felony warrant out of Montana for aggravated assault, aggravated battery, and strangulation. Later, it was also discovered that there was an agent warrant for the individual that the probation officer had put out. It was also discovered through the Idaho Department of Corrections website that the individual was an Idaho Department of Corrections fugitive. All units searched for a few more hours before giving up the search for the individual. It was decided that we would leave the individual’s vehicle and watch to see if he’d returned to it.

That’s when I took up the position just south of Menan Lorenzo Highway off of Yellowstone Highway, watching the stop sign. Approximately an hour passed by, and other units had to respond to another call, leaving me as the only Deputy watching the vehicle.

I was watching the intersection when I saw the suspect vehicle approach the intersection, go through the stop sign, failing to stop, turn east on 4200, and accelerated to a high rate of speed. I went out after the vehicle when I got 4200. I could see no taillights, so I continued down 4200 when I went around the bend and started heading south on 4200. I still could not see any taillights, but I had informed corporal McRae and Deputy Hall that the vehicle had left the area, and I had missed it and it was possibly going down 4200 east southbound. As I approach the intersection of 500 north and 4200 east, Deputy Hall approached it at the same time. Deputy Hall went south, continuing on 4200, and I went east on 500 north to see if I could locate the vehicle. I was at approximately 4400 E. when Corporal McRae was at 300 north and 4200 E. When he saw the vehicle run the stop sign at 4200 east and 300 north and turn west going into the city, Cpl. McRae was able to get in behind the vehicle and get the vehicle up to a speed of 98 miles an hour. Officer Kraning with the Rigby Police Department was also able to get a high rate of speed in the 90s. Corporal McRae and Officer Kraning initiated their traffic lights to try to make a traffic stop when the vehicle accelerated even faster. Corporal McRae stated the individual was failing to yield. I asked what the traffic conditions were and what the speed was. Cpl. McRae stated that there was little to no traffic speeds were in the 90s. I asked Corporal McRae if he was in pursuit, and he said he was.

I continued down 4400 E. over to 4500 E. and went south when the pursuing unit stated that the vehicle had gotten off at the 318 off of Highway 20 and was traveling eastbound on the county line road. I was able to get to 4500 E. and County line, where I got into position to spike the vehicle. I was waiting for the pursuing units to get to my location when Cpl. McRae stated the vehicle turned south into Bonneville County on 4300 E. I had Cpl. McRae advise of traffic conditions and speed, which was no traffic speed, still in the 90s. I returned my spike strips to my vehicle and continued south from the County line on 4500 to Highway 26. I had dispatch contact Bonneville and inform them that we were in pursuit in their county and ask permission to spike the vehicle. When I arrived at Highway 26, Cpl. McRae informed Dispatch they were traveling east on highway 26, no traffic speeds in the 90s. I asked dispatch if we had received approval from Bonneville County to spike the vehicle, and they were still trying to get approval. The suspect vehicle and pursuing deputies passed by me when Staff Sergeant Gonzales, who had been monitoring, said to spike him. I informed him that it was too late; they had already passed me. We continued east on Highway 26 when the suspect vehicle turned north off of Highway 26, traveling back into Jefferson County on 5000 E. There was no traffic. The speed slowed to 70 miles an hour. He ran through the stop sign at County Line Road and 5000 E. We got to 100 north where he turned east, going into Heise. Speed slowed down into the 50s, no traffic when we turn north on 5050 east. Speeds slowed even further down into the 30s when we came to the bridge, and the suspect vehicle came to a stop. All units moved into position for a felony stop when the suspect jumped out of the vehicle and jumped over the edge of the bridge. The suspect was floating down the river on his back, swimming, and appeared to be physically okay, when he was floating down the river west. We tried to keep our lights on him, but he floated downriver, and we no longer had a visual.

Madison County Sheriff’s Office came out with a drone to see if they could locate the suspect, and Deputy Hall and I took K-9 Bizi and started walking the riverbank. We searched for several hours. Madison County searched with their drone until all their batteries were dead, and then I made the decision to discontinue the search. 

The Jefferson County Sheriff’s office is seeking charges against David Randall Hicks for IC 49-1401 reckless driving, IC 49-1404 felony eluding, and IC 37-2734A possession of drug paraphernalia. Nothing Further at this time.

K9 Cpl A. Cleverley 
Jefferson County Sheriff

Jefferson County Sheriff's Office K9 Deployment Report Reporting Officer: K9 Corporal A. Cleverley and K9 Bizi
Date of Incident: October 22, 2025 
Time of Incident: Approximately 10:58 A.M. 
Location: Highway 20, Mile Marker 309, Bonneville County, Idaho 
Assisting Agency: Idaho State Police
Narrative: On October 22, 2025, at approximately 10:58 A.M., I was contacted by the Idaho State Police requesting assistance with a traffic stop in Bonneville County. Upon arrival at the scene—located on Highway 20 near mile marker 309—I observed an Idaho State Trooper conducting a roadside investigation with the occupants of a stopped vehicle.
I deployed K9 Bizi from my patrol unit to conduct a free-air sniff of the exterior of the vehicle. Beginning at the rear driver's side door, K9 Bizi immediately exhibited alert behavior. As we continued along the driver's side, Bizi sniffed low on the door but maintained his focus and pace. Upon reaching the front of the vehicle, Bizi redirected himself back toward the driver's side, again displaying alert behavior.
Once Trooper Higley had removed the occupants from the vehicle, I initiated a second pass with K9 Bizi. Starting at the front of the vehicle, Bizi moved toward the passenger side and focused on the front passenger door. He sniffed low and then sat, indicating the presence of narcotic odor. When prompted to continue, Bizi refused to move, reinforcing his alert. I quietly rewarded him and proceeded around the front of the vehicle to repeat the pass along the driver's side.
As we approached the rear driver's side door again, Bizi pulled back toward the vehicle, scratched at the door, and sat—once more indicating the presence of narcotic odor. I then removed Bizi from the scene and returned him to my patrol unit.
Following the K9 alert, Idaho State Troopers conducted a search of the vehicle and located substances consistent with narcotics. The occupants were subsequently questioned and taken into custody by the Idaho State Police.
I have no further information to report at this time.

Following K9 Bizi’s alerts, a probable cause search of the vehicle was conducted. During the search, a backpack containing marijuana was located. I have nothing further to report at this time.

On December 14, 2025, at approximately 3:20 PM, Rigby Police units were dispatched to 182 S. State Street, the Good to Go gas station in Rigby, Jefferson County, for a report of possible drug activity.
Initial Observations: The reporting party, a cashier at Good to Go, advised that a Hispanic male inside the store was acting strangely, appearing unfocused, and walking around in a manner that made them uncomfortable. The male exited the store, entered a vehicle parked in front of the gas station, and was observed struggling to insert his keys into the ignition before slumping over in the driver’s seat.
Officer Contact: Officer Romrell of the Rigby Police Department made contact with the individual, later identified via Idaho identification card as Gabriel Arteaga Ramirez. During the contact, Ramirez admitted to using methamphetamine the previous day but denied use on the current date. A records check through Dispatch revealed Ramirez’s driver’s license was suspended. Officer Romrell requested additional units to respond.
Deputy Response: Deputy Condon arrived and advised that, based on Ramirez’s admission and erratic behavior, there was reasonable suspicion narcotics were present in the vehicle.
K9 Deployment: Upon arrival, I deployed K9 Bizi to conduct a sniff of the vehicle. Ramirez consented to the dog making contact with the vehicle. Beginning at the front passenger headlight, K9 Bizi was commanded to search. As we moved along the driver’s side, Bizi exhibited alert behavior at the driver’s door, including pulling back, sniffing intensely, sitting, and scratching aggressively — all consistent with trained narcotics detection. Bizi was rewarded and secured back in my patrol vehicle.
Vehicle Search: Based on the K9 alert, a probable cause search was conducted.
•	In the driver’s door, a melted pen commonly used to ingest controlled substances was located.
•	A second melted pen was found in the center console. Ramirez later confirmed to Officer Romrell and Deputy Condon that these items were used to consume methamphetamine.
•	In the trunk, inside a small cubby inside a Spanish Book of Mormon, a plastic bag containing a white crystalline substance was discovered.
Arrest and Charges: Ramirez was taken into custody without incident for:
•	Possession of a Controlled Substance (methamphetamine)
•	Possession of Paraphernalia
•	Driving on a Suspended License
Officer Romrell initiated a separate investigation for Driving under the Influence of Narcotics.
Evidence: The crystalline substance was transported to the Jefferson County Sheriff’s Office, where it tested presumptive positive for methamphetamine.
Disposition: Ramirez was charged under Idaho Code 37-2732 (Possession of a Controlled Substance) and Idaho Code 37-2734A (Possession of Paraphernalia). No further action at this time.

K9 Training Log – Narcotics Detection Practice

Hide 1 – Heroin (3 g)
The first hide consisted of 3 g of real heroin placed beside a refrigerator in the kitchen. I deployed K9 Bizi at the threshold, placed him in a down, and gave the command to search. Bizi moved quickly past the refrigerator along the cabinet line before raising his head and air‑scenting. He turned back toward the refrigerator, investigated the lower portion, worked the odor along the side gap between the fridge and cabinets, and then performed a final response by lying down, indicating he was in the odor of narcotics.

Hide 2 – Cocaine (2 g)
The second hide was 2 g of cocaine concealed behind a mirror in a small bathroom. After opening the door, I brought Bizi inside, removed his leash, and gave the search command. He immediately raised his head and air‑scented toward the ceiling. He worked the odor around the room, moved to the sink, and stood on his hind legs to reach higher scent cones. After pinpointing the source area, he sat and provided a clear final indication.

Hide 3 – Methamphetamine (2 g) in a Soda Can
The third hide was 2 g of methamphetamine placed inside a Sprite can positioned on a cabinet among other soda cans and water bottles. Due to the tight space, I removed Bizi’s leash and allowed him to work freely. He searched along the cabinets, passed the shelf, then abruptly turned back, closed his mouth, and began bracketing the odor around the bottles. He scratched at the correct can and then sat, providing his final indication.

Hide 4 – Marijuana (14 g)
The fourth hide consisted of 14 g of marijuana placed beneath a floor grate in a small custodian closet. After giving the search command, Bizi entered, checked the wall, then moved toward the floor. He sniffed directly over the grate and then laid down on top of it, indicating he was in the odor of narcotics.

Hide 5 – Article Search (5 g Meth) in Six Boxes
The fifth hide involved an article search of six small boxes containing 5 g of methamphetamine. I deployed Bizi, placed him in a down, removed his leash, and gave the search command. He initially ran past the boxes, bumping several into a pile. I reset him at the start and encouraged a slower, methodical search. He then placed his paws on one box, bit at it briefly, and provided a focused stare, indicating the presence of narcotics in that box.

Hide 6 – Cocaine Scent (Scent Logic) Under Passenger Door
The sixth hide used cocaine scent logic placed in a magnetic container under the passenger door of a vehicle. I gave Bizi the search command and worked him around the vehicle. On the driver side he showed interest in the rear panel, influenced by wind blowing from the south/southeast. I presented the vehicle to help him work the scent cone. On the passenger side he sniffed underneath the vehicle, then focused on the lower door seam and sat, giving his final indication.

Hide 7 – Vehicle Hitch Hide (Marijuana Scent logic)
The seventh hide was placed inside the hitch of a vehicle. While searching a blank vehicle, Bizi pulled away on his own and moved directly to the target vehicle. He sniffed around the hitch area and then sat, providing a clear final indication.

Hide 8 – Magnet Hide Under Driver Door (Meth scent logic)
The eighth hide was placed in a magnetic container under the driver door of a truck. I conducted the search as a free‑air sniff, approaching from the rear. As we passed the driver door, Bizi’s head snapped back and he displayed alert behavior. I released him to work the odor. He checked the rear of the vehicle, returned to the driver side, and after pinpointing the source area, laid down to indicate he was in the odor of narcotics.

Dates of Training: January 9–12, 2026
Type of Training: Basic Obedience, Recall with Conflict, Kennel Conditioning

During our scheduled days off from January 9th through January 12th, 2026, I conducted multiple training sessions with K9 Bizi focusing on basic obedience, recall under conflict, and kennel desensitization.

While in the field behind our residence—an area where Bizi routinely exercises on days off—I introduced a recall conflict using Bizi’s preferred treat. As Bizi was running freely, I observed him abruptly flip his head back and attempt to move toward the treat. When he approached the treat, I issued a recall command. Bizi looked toward me, then back toward the treat, but ultimately complied and returned to my side. Once he completed the recall, I released him to locate and receive the treat as a reward.

Bizi continues to display anxiety related to kennel confinement. To address this, I conducted kennel‑conditioning drills by offering treats and toys to create positive associations. Despite these efforts, Bizi still exhibits resistance and has occasional fits when placed in the kennel. Additional conditioning will be required.

On the remaining training days, I worked Bizi through basic obedience drills including heeling, downing while heeling, and extended down‑stays. All exercises were performed both on‑leash and off‑leash. Bizi responded appropriately to commands and demonstrated continued progress in obedience.

K9 Bizi showed improvement in recall under conflict and maintained consistent performance in basic obedience. Kennel anxiety remains an ongoing issue and will require continued focused training.

K9 Deployment Report – Interagency Assist
Date: January 16, 2026 
Time of Request: 11:11 P.M. 
Time of Deployment: 1:14 P.M. 
Location: FedEx Warehouse, 594 N 4062 E, Jefferson County, Idaho 
Requesting Agency: Idaho State Police / Detective Alexandra Larrea
Reason for Deployment: Suspicious Package – Narcotics Sniff
K9 Team: Cpl Andrew Cleverley / K9 Bizi 
Evidence Seized: One package seized by Idaho State Police

At approximately 11:11 P.M. on January 16, 2026, while in Jefferson County, I received a call forwarded from an Idaho State Police Detective. Detective Larrea advised that ISP had received information regarding a suspicious package and requested a K9 narcotics sniff at the FedEx warehouse located at 594 N 4062 E. Detective Larrea stated that ISP personnel would be on scene to conduct the sniff at approximately 1:00 P.M.

Upon arrival at the FedEx warehouse, ISP personnel showed me the suspect package. I requested that FedEx employees place five boxes, including the suspect box, in a single line with adequate spacing between each package.
I deployed K9 Bizi to the search area and placed him in a down position approximately three feet from the first box. As I began walking down the line of packages, Bizi immediately began sniffing the area and crawled forward toward the first package. Before I reached the end of the line, Bizi broke his down position and moved toward the first package, which is consistent with alert behavior.
I then gave Bizi the command to search the packages. He moved past each package sniffing each package intently, and when he passed the suspect package he exhibited a noticeable head snap sniffed hard and puffed his cheeks but continued to the end of the line. Upon reaching the last package, Bizi quickly returned to the first package, ran past it, and then turned back toward the suspect package. He sniffed the suspect package and sat, indicating he was in the odor of narcotics.
I directed Bizi to continue the search, but he stayed next to the suspect package, scratched at it, and sat again, solidifying his final indication on that package. I rewarded Bizi and returned him to my vehicle.
The suspect package was seized by the Idaho State Police for further investigation. 

Later during the day on 1/16/2026, Idaho State Police transported the seized package back to their office and obtained a search warrant to open and examine its contents. Upon opening the parcel, investigators discovered that the outer box had been heavily glued shut. After removing the adhesive material, they located a secondary box concealed inside the larger box. The space between the two boxes was filled with spray foam insulation and fiberglass insulation.
Investigators continued to open the inner box and found it was also sealed with glue and surrounded by additional spray foam and fiberglass insulation. Once they gained access to the interior of the secondary box, they located a vacuum sealed bag containing two powdered substances one white and one pink. Field testing of both substances returned presumptive positive results for cocaine.
The white powder weighed approximately 482.5 grams, and the pink powder weighed approximately 27 grams, for a combined total weight of 509.5 grams (1.13 pounds). Idaho State Police entered the controlled substances into evidence and are continuing their investigation.
Nothing further at this time.
K9 Cpl A. Cleverley
Jefferson County Sheriff

On March 5th, 2026, at approximately 2:33 P.M., I was dispatched to mile marker 322 on Highway 20 in Jefferson County to assist the Idaho State Police (ISP) with a K9 sniff of a vehicle. ISP trooper C. Hanish advised they had reasonable suspicion to believe the driver was under the influence of intoxicating substances based on her observed behavior.
Upon arrival, an ISP trooper C. Hanish informed me they intended to remove the driver, the sole occupant of the vehicle, and conduct Standardized Field Sobriety Tests (SFSTs). As I approached the vehicle with K9 Bizi, the driver spontaneously stated to the trooper, “Yeah, search it.”
I positioned K9 Bizi at the front passenger-side headlight and placed him in a down. As soon as Bizi was placed in the down position, he crawled toward the passenger side of the vehicle, breaking his down and displaying alert behavior. I maintained control of his leash and gave him the command to search.
Bizi immediately got up, moved down the passenger side of the vehicle, and then crossed in front of the vehicle in coordination with my movement. We continued down the driver side, with Bizi searching high and low along the vehicle exterior. As we rounded the rear of the vehicle and returned up the passenger side, Bizi raised his head toward an open window. He sniffed around the window, showing alert behavior, then stood on his hind legs, sniffed inside the open window, and immediately sat, indicating he was in the odor of narcotics.
I attempted to move Bizi away from the indication to continue the search; however, he refused to leave the area, further solidifying his indication.
ISP placed the driver into custody and advised her of her Miranda rights. I identified myself and informed her that K9 Bizi is trained to indicate on the odor of narcotics. I asked why Bizi might have indicated on her vehicle. The driver stated her brother in law had purchased the vehicle approximately three weeks earlier from a man in Provo, Utah, and that the previous owner may have been living in the vehicle. She stated that, to her knowledge, there was nothing illegal inside the vehicle.
A search of the vehicle was conducted, and no contraband was located. ISP continued their investigation and requested a Drug Recognition Officer (DRO) to respond.
I have nothing further at this time.

K9 Training Report

Handler:
K9: Bizi
Dates of Training: February 10–13, 2026
Type of Training: Crate Conditioning, Recall, Down‑in‑Motion, Duration Downs

Narrative

During scheduled days off from February 10th through February 13th, I conducted multiple training sessions with K9 Bizi focusing on crate training, recall, down‑in‑motion, and extended duration downs.

Crate training remains an ongoing area of development. Bizi will enter the kennel on command; however, he continues to show discomfort when left alone for extended periods. Training sessions included short‑duration confinement paired with positive reinforcement to build a more neutral association with the kennel.

Recall work was conducted in an open field. Bizi consistently returned when called and showed no issues with basic recall. To increase difficulty, I threw a ball into the field when Bizi could not see its landing point. While moving toward the ball, I issued a down‑in‑motion command. When the ball was not visible, Bizi performed a clean down‑in‑motion at approximately the halfway point between me and the ball. When the ball was visible, he initially struggled to comply and required e‑collar corrections. After several sessions, he began responding reliably even with the visible distraction.

I also worked Bizi on stationary duration downs. He completed a three‑minute down and a five‑minute down at approximately 15 feet from me. Bizi maintained position appropriately during both exercises and demonstrated good control.

Summary

Bizi showed strong performance in recall, down‑in‑motion under moderate distraction, and extended duration downs. Crate conditioning continues to improve, though he still displays discomfort when left alone for longer periods. Continued focused work on kennel neutrality is recommended.

K9 Training Report

Handler:
K9: Bizi
Dates of Training: February 18–21, 2026
Type of Training: Jump Work, Obedience, Heeling

Narrative

During scheduled days off from February 18th through February 21st, I conducted multiple training sessions with K9 Bizi focusing on jump work and obedience.

To address Bizi’s tendency to go around obstacles rather than jump, I set up a table in the yard to create a controlled jump scenario. The exercise required Bizi to jump onto the table, move across to the opposite side, and perform a down. While on leash, Bizi completed the jump and down reliably. When working off leash, he attempted to go around the table instead of jumping, indicating the need for continued reinforcement of the behavior without physical guidance.

Heeling work was also conducted throughout the training period. Bizi performed well both on and off leash, maintaining position and responding appropriately to verbal and physical cues.

Summary

Bizi showed solid obedience and heeling performance. Jump work continues to improve, with strong on‑leash compliance and ongoing development needed for consistent off‑leash execution.

K9 Training Report

Handler:
K9: Bizi
Dates of Training: February 26–March 1, 2026
Type of Training: Heeling, Kennel Conditioning, Recall, Door‑Pop Response

Narrative

During scheduled days off from February 26th through March 1st, I conducted multiple training sessions with K9 Bizi focusing on obedience, kennel neutrality, recall, and door‑pop drills.

Heeling work was performed both on and off leash. Bizi maintained consistent position, responded appropriately to cues, and demonstrated reliable control regardless of environment or distraction level.

Kennel training was incorporated to continue improving Bizi’s comfort and neutrality with confinement. Sessions included placing him in the kennel for short periods and rewarding calm behavior. Bizi continues to show progress but still requires ongoing conditioning to reduce his discomfort with being left alone in the kennel.

Recall work was conducted in various contexts, including while Bizi was playing with the other dogs at home. His recall remains strong; he consistently disengages from play and returns promptly when called.

Door‑pop drills were completed using the patrol vehicle. I hid at different locations on the property, activated the door pop, and required Bizi to locate me. He showed enthusiasm for the exercise and worked methodically to determine my location. When unable to locate me, Bizi returned to the patrol vehicle on his own and laid down inside until I returned. This behavior is beneficial for accidental door pops, demonstrating that he will default back to the vehicle if he cannot find the handler.

Summary

Bizi performed well in obedience, recall, and door‑pop response. Kennel conditioning continues to improve, and his default behavior of returning to the patrol vehicle when unsure of handler location is a positive safety behavior.

Building Search Training – Hallway and Door‑Clearing Drill

During a building‑search training scenario, I worked with two deputies positioned in a stack outside the hallway. I moved between them—one deputy to my rear and one facing forward—and released Bizi into the hallway to begin a controlled search and clear doorways.

Using a 30‑foot line, I attempted to slow Bizi’s pace and guide him to search each doorway methodically. Bizi resisted this pattern; he attempted to pull ahead and run the full length of the hallway rather than work each door individually. I reset him by bringing him back to the start point and gradually feeding out line to encourage a slower, more deliberate search. This drill is not one we have practiced extensively, and Bizi showed confusion about the expectations. Continued repetitions will be needed to build clarity and consistency.

After the controlled‑line repetitions, I released Bizi for an independent hallway search. He moved door‑to‑door, checking each threshold for human odor consistent with a concealed suspect. The hallway was blank, and he did not show any alert or indication on any door.

Second Hide – Truck Hitch - meth 109g

The second source was hidden in the hitch area of a pickup truck, with several treats scattered around the vehicle as distractions. I started Bizi at the front passenger‑side headlight, gave the command to search, and worked clockwise around the vehicle. As we reached the rear, Bizi rose onto his hind legs to sniff the tailgate, then dropped down and pushed underneath the vehicle toward the hitch. His behavior was consistent with pinpointing odor, and I called the source. The organizer confirmed Bizi was correct.

Third Hide – Spare Tire Under SUV - cocaine - 335 g 

The third source was placed in the spare tire mounted underneath an SUV. I deployed Bizi at the front passenger‑side headlight and gave the search command. We moved across the front of the vehicle, down the driver side, and to the rear. At the back, Bizi sniffed the tailgate, then sat, followed by laying down and crawling underneath the vehicle toward the spare tire. This behavior indicated he was in the odor of narcotics. I called the source, and the organizer confirmed accuracy.

Fourth Hide – Front Passenger Headlight of SUV - marijuana - 25 g 

The fourth source was hidden behind the front passenger‑side headlight of an SUV. I placed Bizi in a down at the front passenger headlight and gave the search command. He moved toward the center of the vehicle, sniffed briefly, and sat, indicating odor. When I attempted to move him with light leash pressure, he refused to leave the area and then laid down. I called the indication, and the organizer advised “pinpoint.” I repositioned toward the passenger side and tapped around the wheel well and headlight area. Bizi sniffed the area again and laid down, confirming his final response. The organizer stated he was correct.

---

Overall Performance

Bizi performed well on all four hides, locating each source accurately and showing strong, consistent alert and final response behaviors despite distractions and varying hide placements.

The decoy was positioned approximately ten feet up in a tree, with wind blowing to the northeast at an estimated 30 mph. I deployed K9 Bizi into an open field located just northeast of the suspect’s position. After issuing three verbal warnings, I released Bizi to apprehend.

Bizi moved through the area and came close to the suspect’s location several times. Each time, he flipped his head up into the scent cone, but the strong wind pushed odor down the tree line to the north, causing him to follow the blown odor away from the actual source. After observing this pattern, I moved closer to the suspect’s location and reset the scenario.

On the second deployment, Bizi again followed the wind‑carried odor north. When he reached the end of the long line, I began moving him back toward the suspect to the south, allowing him to work back into the true scent cone. As we approached the tree, Bizi appeared to recognize the presence of the suspect. He circled the base of the tree, attempting to locate an access point, before sitting and barking, indicating he had located the suspect.

At that time, the suspect climbed down from the tree. Bizi immediately engaged and conducted a muzzle apprehension, maintaining control until the scenario was concluded.

K9 Training Log – June 1st

Long‑Line Searches with Tactical Team

Brought K9 Bizi into the staging area and positioned the tactical team with a designated lethal‑cover officer and secondary cover. After giving three verbal commands, I released Bizi on a 30‑foot long line.

Bizi searched a large open area and worked up to a corner. I downed him at that position and moved the team up to his location. Once the team was set, I released Bizi again out to the full length of the line. I downed him a second time and advanced the team forward.

On the next release, Bizi’s head snapped toward a room, indicating a change in behavior. He entered the room independently and made contact with the suspect, completing the apprehension portion of the drill.

---

Muscle‑Punch Drill with Soccer Ball

Conducted muzzle‑conditioning work in an open field using a soccer ball. The ball was kicked toward Bizi, and he engaged it immediately, delivering repeated muzzle punches and driving it with his muzzle. Behavior was consistent with the purpose of the drill: building forward drive and impact confidence.

---

Muzzle Fight on Long Line

Brought Bizi in for a muzzle‑fight scenario with an agitator. While on a long line, the agitator advanced toward Bizi. Bizi engaged without hesitation, initiating muzzle strikes and maintaining forward pressure. I fed line out gradually as the agitator moved backward, allowing Bizi to continue driving the fight deeper into the room. Bizi performed this drill effectively.

---

Building Search with Muzzle

Brought Bizi to the building entry, gave commands, and released him to search for a concealed suspect. Bizi moved up the stairwell into a room, searched the area thoroughly, located the suspect, and engaged with muzzle strikes. He completed the drill as expected.

---

Second Building Search – Blacked‑Out Room

The second scenario involved a completely dark room with no ambient light. I brought Bizi to the doorway, issued commands, and released him. Bizi showed no hesitation entering the dark environment. He moved throughout the room, located the suspect, and engaged with muzzle strikes, effectively completing the drill.

K9 Training Report — June 2nd

Tie‑Back Release and Recall Drills — Bite Suit

During tie‑back apprehension drills, an agitator wearing a bite suit was positioned inside the training area. After giving verbal commands for the suspect to comply and receiving no compliance, I moved into position and released K9 Bizi for an apprehension. Once Bizi engaged the bite, I issued the out command followed by a down command.

During the first several repetitions, Bizi remained on the bite and required E‑collar assistance to complete the out and transition into the down. After a few repetitions, Bizi began releasing on the first command and immediately going into a down without additional correction.

Once Bizi was in the down, I recalled him to my side. He returned cleanly and consistently. After the initial E‑collar assistance during the first few outs, Bizi required no further corrections for the remainder of the drill and performed each recall effectively.

---

Fence Drill — Bite Suit and Toy Reward System

A second drill was conducted using a fence barrier. An agitator positioned behind the fence remained visible to Bizi while Bizi was tied back to a pole. Bizi was able to bark and show aggression toward the agitator but could not make physical contact.

When Bizi displayed appropriate aggression and forward drive toward the agitator, he was rewarded with a toy. I then gave the release command for the toy. The agitator re‑engaged to draw Bizi’s focus back to him. The purpose of the drill was to reinforce that Bizi must leave the toy and refocus on the agitator behind the fence.

Bizi performed this reliably. After approximately six toy presentations, all dropped around him, Bizi consistently disengaged from each toy and redirected his focus to the agitator.

As the drill progressed, a second agitator in a bite suit moved closer to Bizi. The objective was for Bizi to ignore the closer individual and maintain focus on the primary agitator behind the fence. Bizi successfully maintained target discrimination, repeatedly choosing the agitator behind the fence and leaving the bite‑suit agitator alone.

Eventually, the bite‑suit agitator moved close enough that Bizi had to shift his position around him. Bizi continued to ignore the closer agitator and remained committed to the primary target. He was rewarded at the conclusion of the drill with a live sleeve, simulating a live human bite.

K9 Training Documentation – June 3rd

1. Long‑Line Building Search – Bite Suit & Tactical Team

During a long‑line building search with a tactical team, I positioned my team around the perimeter and at the doorway before giving commands to release K9 Bizi. Five teams had already run the scenario, and the agitator location had not been changed. As a result, odor saturation inside the structure was significant.

Upon release, Bizi drove to the end of the line and began barking, bypassing an open doorway. I moved up to him and directed the team to clear rooms. Throughout the search, Bizi continued pushing forward toward the source, showing a strong desire to reach the odor rather than conduct methodical room‑to‑room clearing.

Bizi ultimately moved upstairs, located the agitator, and made a successful apprehension.

Instructor Feedback:
The instructor noted that Bizi detected the suspect’s odor immediately upon entering the building and displayed clear alert behavior. Because he was already in odor, he did not feel compelled to search intermediate rooms. The scenario was completed successfully.

Training Notes:
Use slower, deliberate search commands and employ redirection tools—such as tossing bolts or coins into rooms—to encourage room‑specific searching when Bizi is already in odor.

---

2. Open‑Area Search – Bite Suit

Scenario involved an escaped suspect inside a large fenced compound with multiple shops and vehicles. I deployed Bizi at the open gate and immediately recognized numerous elevated hiding locations.

After giving three commands, I released Bizi to search. He quickly displayed alert behavior—head snap, upward sniffing—and pulled north along the fence line. At a truck, his head flipped back south, and he moved toward the vehicle. I advised my team that Bizi was in odor and followed his direction of travel.

Rounding a corner, I observed another head snap toward a shop area. Bizi pulled decisively into the space, worked with his head high, then turned east, drove between containers, and made a successful apprehension.

I called Bizi out, removed him from the bite, and secured the suspect.

Instructor Feedback:
Recommended using a down command prior to moving in after the out, and emphasized slowing movement and applying defensive tactics more deliberately.

---

3. Violent Felon Encounter – Knife Threat in Building

Upon entering the building, an OIC briefed me that cover officers were positioned down the hallway with the suspect. As I rounded the corner, I observed a cover officer with a firearm pointed downrange. I moved in behind him, took the hallway, and issued commands to the suspect, who was facing away.

As she moved, I prepared to release Bizi. She suddenly turned, revealing a knife. I issued additional commands; she threw the knife and charged toward us. I released Bizi for apprehension.

After Bizi secured the suspect, I called him off, issued commands to the suspect to show her hands and get to her knees, and positioned Bizi at my side. The apprehension team moved in and took her into custody.

Instructor Feedback:
Scenario was handled well. Only recommendation was to allow the suspect to advance farther down the hallway before release to create greater distance from the discarded weapon.

---

4. Drag Training – Passive Suspect

I deployed Bizi on a 30‑foot line toward a passive suspect lying with hands concealed. After presenting aggression, I released Bizi down the line. He made contact on the suspect’s left upper arm with a full, committed bite.

Once the bite was confirmed, I began drag training—pulling Bizi and the suspect toward me. With each drag, Bizi maintained the bite, readjusted deeper as needed, and continued to drive forward. The drill was completed successfully.

---

5. Home Search – Passive Suspect

I deployed Bizi to the doorway of a residence. Upon my first command, the suspect revealed himself with hands raised. I could see his hands were empty but could not confirm his waistband.

I issued multiple commands for him to lift his collar and expose his waistband; he did not comply. I directed him to exit the home toward me and my cover officer. I placed Bizi in a down and advised the suspect that any threatening movement would result in K9 deployment.

My cover officer provided security while I moved in and took the suspect into custody without incident.

After the scenario, the agitator allowed Bizi to engage in muzzle work. Bizi demonstrated strong fight drive and forward pressure.

During a building‑entry scenario involving a burglary suspect, I deployed K9 Bizi at the doorway. Per the instructor’s direction, I placed Bizi in a down position in the threshold, created distance, and moved to a position of cover while maintaining control with a long line.

Once positioned, I issued the command for Bizi to search the building. Bizi immediately located the first suspect approximately 30 feet inside and engaged with a bite. As soon as Bizi made contact, the suspect removed the long line from Bizi’s collar, which resulted in a temporary loss of physical control.

A second suspect then emerged, yelling and refusing to comply with commands. I issued multiple verbal commands for him to show his hands, but he did not comply. I also gave commands to the first suspect—who was under Bizi’s bite—to move into view; he stated he could not due to Bizi’s hold.

I recalled Bizi from the first bite. As Bizi returned toward me, he observed the second suspect and redirected, engaging him. The second suspect then moved with Bizi into an adjacent room.

My cover officer and I proceeded methodically through the structure, clearing hallways and rooms until we reached the first suspect, who was taken into custody. We then moved into the room where Bizi was engaged with the second suspect. The cover officer took that suspect into custody, and I removed Bizi from the bite.

Instructor Feedback

• Maintain the down command at the doorway, then take cover further back to maximize safety and control.
• Improve the speed and clarity of recalling Bizi off the initial bite.

First started with the suspect/ agitator laying on the ground inside a building, as if they were passed out. I used a 15-foot-long line and gave commands to the suspect to show me her hands. The suspect didn’t move. I gave K9 Prop the apprehend command and sent Prop in using the log line to show him down to help place a safe bite. Prop bit the left forearm, and the suspect remained still. Using Prop's harness and long line, I dragged the suspect down the hall. This training is for the case someone is unconscious, and it’s not safe to go in and detain the suspect; I can use my K9 to drag the suspect away from a weapon to a safe spot to detain. I used the jaw breaker to remove Prop from the bite and pulled him away.

 

I gave the suspect commands to stand up, and the suspect stood up and ran away. I sent Prop to apprehend the suspect, and Prop bit the upper right arm. Prop held and continues to hold while the suspect tried to fight. I told the suspect to hold still and was able to get the Prop on the first command to put the bite down without further contact with the suspect. I had the suspect step away from Prop and stand still. Prop stayed and didn’t break his down. I went and started to pat the suspect down, and the suspect tried to fight me, and Prop broke him down and bit the suspect again. This time I hard-outted Prop with a choke-off, and we chased the suspect out of sight.

 

Moved outside and off leash, I downed Prop and started giving commands for the suspect to come out. The suspect came out and came toward me like I was telling her to do. The suspect then turned and ran away, and I gave Prop his command to apprehend. The suspect stopped running with her hands up before Prop got to her, so I gave Prop the down command, and Prop downed without making contact with the suspect. I recalled Prop to heal, and Prop came back to me and healed. I gave additional commands for the suspect to come to me, and the suspect again took off. I sent Prop to apprehend, and Prop bit the right upper arm and knocked the suspect to the ground. Prop kept holding on while the suspect kept fighting. When the suspect got to her feet, I 3 phased out Prop, and he again let go and downed the suspect without biting her again. I had the suspect remain where she was and recalled Prop to heal; Prop healed, and I leashed Prop. I had the suspect walk out of site and Prop was verbally praised back to my patrol car.

Verbal Out:

Overall Behavior:  
Bizi performed well throughout the session. Drive remained high, but obedience stayed intact. No issues noted.

Next Steps / Recommendations

Increase environmental distractions in future sessions to further proof the behaviors.

Maintain consistency with verbal cues to preserve the strong out response.

Around 0900 Rocky had come inside the house after being let out to take a break after having been fed. Everything seemed fine with him. When he came inside, he went to Lynne who was sitting in a chair in the kitchen. She was petting him on his head and he was wagging his tail. She started to pet him under his chin on his neck, wrapping her arm around him some, I noticed she leaned in towards him some. At this point I noticed his body language change, he stopped wagging his tail and he laid his ears back. Before I could get up from the table where I was sitting about 10 feet away from them, I watched Lynne jerk her head back turning it away from Rocky as he lunged forward and began to bite her on the upper arm. I rushed over towards them calling him off. He stopped as soon as I called him off but he had already bit her several times on the arm. I pulled him to the ground pinning him there while Lynne got up and moved away, I noticed several Bite marks on her arm that were bleeding. Rocky was disciplined for what he had done and placed back inside of his kennel where he normally spends his time.
